title: Cleft Sentences, Ellipsis & Substitution
description: Master cleft sentences (it-cleft, what-cleft), ellipsis and substitution (do/so/not) for Grade 11 — tools for emphasis and economy in writing, with bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Cleft Sentences (It-Cleft & What-Cleft)
topics.concept:
A cleft sentence divides one clause into two to emphasise a particular part.

It-cleft: It + be + (emphasised part) + who/that/which + rest.

  • John called yesterday. → It was John who called yesterday. (emphasis on John)
  • → It was yesterday that John called. (emphasis on the time)

What-cleft (pseudo-cleft): What + clause + be + (emphasised part).

  • I want peace. → What I want is peace.
  • She did her best. → What she did was (to) do her best.

Clefts answer 'which one exactly?' — they pinpoint the key information for the reader.

examples.problem: Make an it-cleft emphasising 'the manager': The manager approved the plan.
examples.solution: It was the manager who approved the plan.

examples.problem: Make a what-cleft: I admire her honesty.

recap: It-cleft: It + be + X + who/that + rest (emphasis on X)
What-cleft: What + clause + be + X (emphasis at the end)

topics.title: Ellipsis & Substitution
topics.concept:
Ellipsis omits words that can be understood from context, avoiding repetition:

  • Verbal: She can sing and (she can) dance.
  • Nominal: I have two pens; you can take one (pen).
  • Clausal: He said he would help, and he did (help).

Substitution replaces a word or phrase with a shorter 'pro-form':

  • do/does/did replaces a verb phrase: She works hard, and so does he.
  • so replaces a clause after think/hope/believe: "Will it rain?" "I think so."
  • not replaces a negative clause: "Is he coming?" "I hope not."
  • one/ones replaces a countable noun: The red shirt and the blue one.

Use these to keep writing tight — but only when the meaning stays clear.

examples.problem: Use ellipsis: He likes tea and he likes coffee.
Substitute: "Has she left?" "I believe she has left."

recap: Ellipsis omits repeated words (verbal, nominal, clausal)
Use them for economy — keep the meaning clear

questions.q: Which is a what-cleft?
options: What surprised me was the result.
questions.explanation: 'What … was …'.

questions.q: Complete the it-cleft: '___ was Riya who topped the class.'
questions.explanation: It-cleft begins with 'It'.

questions.q: Substitute correctly: 'They are tired, and ___.'
questions.explanation: 'so are we' (inversion).

questions.q: Ellipsis: 'She wanted to come but couldn't ___.'
questions.explanation: The verb is understood; 'couldn't' stands alone.

questions.q: 'Will he agree?' 'I think ___.'
questions.explanation: 'I think so' = I think he will agree.

questions.q: Rewrite as it-cleft (emphasis on object): 'I lost my keys.'
options: It was my keys that I lost.
It was I who lost keys.
What I lost was keys it was.
My keys it was that lost I.
questions.explanation: 'It was my keys that I lost.'

questions.q: Which uses 'one' as substitution?
questions.explanation: 'one' replaces the countable noun.

questions.q: 'She left early, and so ___ I.'
questions.explanation: Past tense → 'so did I'.

questions.q: Make a what-cleft: 'I need your help.'
options: What I need is your help.
It is your help that I need.
Both A and B emphasise it.
Your help I need is what.
questions.explanation: Both clefts work; A is the what-cleft.

questions.q: 'Is the shop open?' 'I'm afraid ___.' (it's closed)
questions.explanation: 'I'm afraid not' = it is not open.

questions.q: Ellipsis: 'He can swim, and she can ___ too.'
questions.explanation: Verbal ellipsis allows '(swim)'; the bare form 'swim' is standard if stated.

questions.q: Which sentence is a cleft?
options: It was the noise that woke me.
I was woken by the noise.
questions.explanation: It-cleft emphasising 'the noise'.

questions.q: Rewrite to emphasise the reason: 'He resigned because he was overworked.'
options: It was because he was overworked that he resigned.
It was he who resigned overworked.
Because overworked it was he resigned.
questions.explanation: It-cleft emphasising the reason clause.

questions.q: Spot the error: 'What I like about her are her honesty and warmth.'
options: are → is (notional singular) OR keep 'are' for two nouns
questions.explanation: Style varies: with two coordinated nouns 'are' is acceptable; many prefer 'is'. The item highlights this subtlety.

questions.q: Choose the correct substitution: 'A: She has finished. B: ___ '
questions.explanation: Confirming inversion: 'So has she.'

questions.q: Rewrite with ellipsis: 'You can stay if you want to stay.'
options: You can stay if you want to.
You can stay if you want stay.
You can stay if want you to.
You can if you want stay to.
questions.explanation: Verbal ellipsis after 'to': '…if you want to.'

questions.q: Which is a correctly formed pseudo-cleft?
questions.explanation: Balance with a noun phrase: 'encouragement'.

questions.q: Choose the correct response with 'not': 'A: Do you think they'll cancel it? B: ___ '
questions.explanation: 'I hope not' substitutes the negative clause.

questions.q: Rearrange into an it-cleft: 'that / it / patience / was / saw / her / through'
options: It was patience that saw her through.
It was that patience saw her through.
Patience it was that saw her through.
That it was patience saw through her.
questions.explanation: 'It was patience that saw her through.'

questions.q: Which sentence best uses ellipsis for economy?
options: Some students passed the test and some students failed the test.
Some students passed the test and some failed.
Some passed and some students failed the test.
Some students the test passed and some failed it the test.
questions.explanation: 'Some passed and some failed' omits the repeated subject and object cleanly.

outcomes: Use ellipsis to omit repeated elements
Use substitution with do/does/did, so and not

intro.en: Three devices let you control emphasis and economy. A cleft sentence splits one idea to spotlight a part ('It was Ram who broke it'). Ellipsis leaves out words the reader can supply ('She can sing and (she can) dance'). Substitution replaces a phrase with a small word ('I think so'). Together they make writing both forceful and concise.
intro.hi: तीन युक्तियाँ आपको बल और संक्षिप्तता पर नियंत्रण देती हैं। cleft sentence एक विचार को बाँटकर किसी भाग पर ध्यान केंद्रित करता है ('It was Ram who broke it')। Ellipsis उन शब्दों को छोड़ देता है जिन्हें पाठक स्वयं समझ ले ('She can sing and (she can) dance')। Substitution एक वाक्यांश को छोटे शब्द से बदल देता है ('I think so')। मिलकर ये लेखन को सशक्त और संक्षिप्त बनाते हैं।

real_life.situation:
Three ways to say the same thing:

Plain: I need rest most of all.

Cleft: What I need most is rest.
real_life.why: The what-cleft pushes 'rest' to the end, where it lands with emphasis. Writers and speakers use clefts to highlight exactly the word that matters — a skill prized in essays and debate.

rule_box.html:
DeviceFormExample
It-cleftIt + be + X + who/that…It was John who called.
What-cleftWhat … + be + XWhat I need is rest.
Ellipsisomit repeated wordsShe can sing and (can) dance.
Substitutiondo/so/notHe works hard and so do I.
rule_box.formula: Cleft = split to emphasise · Ellipsis = omit · Substitution = replace
rule_box.example: It was rest that I needed. = What I needed was rest.

quick_test.q: 'It was Ravi who won' is an example of:
quick_test.explanation: 'It + be + Ravi + who…' is an it-cleft.

common_mistakes.note: Use 'who' for a person in an it-cleft.

common_mistakes.wrong: What I need is to rest. (awkward) / I rest.
common_mistakes.note: Balance the what-cleft with a noun phrase.

common_mistakes.wrong: She can sing and dance she can.
common_mistakes.note: Use ellipsis cleanly, not awkward repetition.

common_mistakes.wrong: He works hard and so I do.
common_mistakes.right: He works hard and so do I.

error_detection.sentence: He is tired and so I am.
error_detection.correct: He is tired and so am I.

error_detection.correct: She can drive and fly a plane.

reading.passage: It was determination that carried the team through. What they lacked in skill, they made up in spirit. "Do you think we can win?" asked the youngest. "I believe so," replied the captain. The others nodded; so did the coach. In the end, it was not talent but teamwork that mattered, and everyone knew it.

questions.q: Identify the it-cleft sentences and what each emphasises.
questions.answer: 'It was determination that carried the team' (emphasis on determination); 'it was not talent but teamwork that mattered' (emphasis on teamwork).

questions.q: Find the what-cleft and explain its effect.
questions.answer: 'What they lacked in skill, they made up in spirit' — it contrasts and emphasises 'spirit'.

questions.q: Identify one substitution.
questions.answer: 'I believe so' (so = we can win); 'so did the coach' (so did = also nodded).

speaking: It was her smile that won everyone over.
He left early, and so did I.

writing.prompt: Write five sentences about a memorable day, using one it-cleft, one what-cleft, one example of ellipsis, and two of substitution (so/do).
writing.example: It was the rain that made it special. What I remember most is the laughter. We danced and sang. They were happy, and so were we. "Was it fun?" "I think so."

micro_quiz.q: Complete the what-cleft: '___ I admire is your courage.'
Ellipsis: 'I bought a red pen and a blue ___.'
'Is it raining?' 'I hope ___.' (you don't want rain)
micro_quiz.explanation: 'I hope not' = I hope it is not raining.

challenge.q: Rewrite as an it-cleft emphasising the time: 'We met in 2019.'
options: It was in 2019 that we met.
It was we who met in 2019.
What we did in 2019 was meet.
In 2019 it was that we met.
She passed the exam, and so I did.
She passed the exam, and so did I.
She passed the exam, and I did so passed.
She passed the exam, so did so I.
challenge.explanation: 'and so did I' inverts the auxiliary.

challenge.q: Choose the best ellipsis: 'He promised to call, and he called.'
options: He promised to call, and he did.
He promised to call, and called he.
He promised to call, and so.
He promised to call, and did he.
challenge.explanation: 'and he did' uses clausal ellipsis/substitution with 'did'.
